questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Personal connection to the destination (heritage / friends there/ etc.)

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: Personal connection because of both heritage and friends, as well as academic opportunities in having the privilege in attending a university of both high historic and academic status. Another aspect was the concrete possibility of housing in a university city where cultures and nationalities meet in one single campus-like town, where safety and comfort, as well as engagement with and discovery of new environments by virtue of one's abilities and willingness to socialize are greatly prioritized. Going abroad to practice language skills was equally central to the choosing, not to mention the sheer personal and administrative growth in approaching a new opportunity with care and responsibility.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: I wasn't afraid to ask whenever I was confused or lacked support in areas, but if one isn't necessarily accustomed to doing that, maybe by it being too intimidating, then I'd assume one would have a hard time finding all the right information. There were times where I felt like I was in the unknown and approaching a situation completely unaware of what would await me, in a sense.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer:
I managed to "book" a physical appointment with a person in charge, which she suggested as she might've sensed my unknowing and wanted to cram every little question I had - which amounted to a continuous email correspondence - into one single sit-down where I could see and hear the person in front of me as well as the university itself.
There were also welcoming days - one amphi seminar-like class, where students would be "welcomed" and receive information, although much of this was vague information and much of it of social relevance than academic which I struggled with in the beginning. I ended up asking my new classmates - when I in fact enrolled in the courses - for information because it was much more helpful and comfortable.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer: Easy as I had contacts in the Cité Universitaire, but that was fortunate and privileged. Though I would always recommend asking anyone and everyone, some might be able to help more than possibly perceived.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer: Make sure to know the most affordable and easy mode of travel to and from university + knowing the time of said travel to and from. Find libraries around your housing, that's both comfortable and practical.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: I had to be selected and approved for even applying to the host institution. Between that and actually applying, the procedure was a little demanding and at times confusing, because a lot had to be done of bureaucratic measures, but once all was filled out, it was pretty smooth. I had to fill out the application online which was long and within a network system that seemed outdated, although it worked fine. It was primarily ticking off boxes, so no motivational letter was necessary, but I had to attach files with evidence of both language skills, learning agreement (if I remember correctly), passport and former grades.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: There was provided several step-by-step guides to work and navigate the system, which was helpful.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: I had to work around timing and planning issues, but I received help in person from a person in charge after meeting with her physically, and eventually I got the classes I wanted, somewhat. The procedure in getting an Online Learning Agreement and a pre-approval was tricky, and felt isolating at times.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Talk to people! Ask questions, no matter how small or big.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA classes while you were on exchange *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: I managed to get both L1, L2 and L3, meaning first year, second year and third year courses in a total of five courses.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: It differed in pace and treating of curriculum. It seemed that there wasn't any mandatory reading, and courses depended on mouth to ear from teacher to student. Very by-heart learning as in one would listen to a teacher and take notes. Not much engaging which is completely different from my home university.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
1. Histoire de la Photographie
2. Archéologie et Arts de l'Afrique
3. Art et Mondialisation
4. Art du XXè siècle
5. Histoire de la Mode

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
Art et Mondialisation by virtue of the teacher, Lotte Arndt, and the building/planning of the course with its treated subjects and themes.
Histoire de la Photographie I would recommend for first year students.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: Some home furnishing like pillows, pillowcases and a tray to carry things to and from communal kitchen. As for academic context, the French system requires pens and paper etc. as computers aren't used for any tests and/or exams.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: Can't think of any, but you can find cheaper alternatives to many things of same quality.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I didn't participate in anything, but it was widely encouraged and it seemed easy and practical.

questions.question: What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Sports mainly. Also political protests and rallies, as well as exhibitions, lectures, events and student trips that were encouraged and broad to attention (although mainly by mail and/or flyers available in the halls etc.)

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: Being social in any way shape or form, to the ability and extent that one is capable of. Being social can be intimidating, but is very much what can hold everything together and make the stay worth it in the long run. Don't be afraid to put yourself out there. There are sports, but also engaging in group chats to plan get-togethers and activities such as museum going, bar hopping (can be done alcohol-free), game nights and karaokes etc. Taking walks around the city is also a major must, as you get movement, cognitive recognition of surroundings, especially when paying attention, learning several neighborhoods. Grocery shopping and meal prepping together is also fulfilling and a fun way to do everyday things. Cinema, as in going to the movies, either alone or with someone is also great. One shouldn't be afraid of solidarity either.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: Museums, parks, monuments and taking non-planned walks, seeing the nooks and crannies of the city.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: Very. Stay open and curious. Know your boundaries but don't take everything personal. Engage with people, not machines, make it a habit of asking people for help.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: Be honest and daring enough to get out of your shell, as long as you don't hurt yourself or push yourself too hard, beyond personal boundaries etc. Find one or two people, or a small group to be around and be comfortable with.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: Not challenging, only uplifting and teaching me new ways of approaching situations, especially academic.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: Food and the particular culture of enjoyment in life. Also the city's life in general, bustling both day and night. I appreciate Paris' cultural offers and the multicultural side(s) of the city. Language also, of course.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer: It can be tough, but social network will help, and trusting oneself, preferably without having too high standards or expectations towards oneself. Making mistakes and not understanding everything is normal and to be expected. The only thing you have to do is show up, both for yourself and physically in being present. Don't isolate yourself, and remember that you're for the most part on exchange to learn and experience, not to perform and perfect.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: Write mails or show up and ask questions. Don't be late for classes, in fact, in the beginning when you're still getting the hang of things, be a little early. Don't stress and remember to take notes, however manageable. Have access to a printer and several libraries.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: The language development, learning that I was able to complete this semester academically and the housing in the Cité Universitaire.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: Doing oral presentations in each course, in French, when I havn't been much accustomed to that kind at home, much less in another language. The bureaucratic procedures, with three individual institutional procedures to navigate, Erasmus+ and the amount of steps to take in relation to that is on that list as well. I had a hard time joggling both exchange, housing, academic procedures and responsibilities all while being on actual exchange and going to school, being social etc.. The different elements took time away from the other elements, and my stay in general. But this is a mental issue, mostly.

questions.question: Any other comments?
Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
